prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned body of Romanian-language prose, with poetry as its ground, in which memory, the body and dream are built into a cosmological architecture that renews the means of inward and fantastic narrative.

statement.case_for: My configuration does not change: Cărtărescu remains my single preferred laureate. After reading the exchange I rest the case on the whole-oeuvre test, not on the shared first places, which are not evidence of merit. The voice is recognisable at the level of the sentence and of the whole book. Blinding and Solenoid, as publicly known, show one imaginative scheme (body, memory, dream, cosmology) developed across very large structures. The chair asks what would show that the late work deepens the early project. Solenoid is a later large novel that, as far as public knowledge goes, takes up the same materials in a different construction rather than copying the earlier book. That is a reception-based reading, not a verified one. The poetry and shorter prose point to a project that is not confined to the long novels. I have refined the citation in response to the chair's questions. It names prose as the core with poetry as ground, since the translation record is thinnest for the poetry. It avoids national symbolism and does not claim to renew 'the novel' in general. It describes inward and fantastic narrative as a form of imagination. The prize honours a whole body of work and not one book. On that basis his is the most coherent and consolidated body of work on this shortlist that I can assess, and I would still want colleagues to push on the weak points.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged. My judgment of the Romanian prose rests on translation reception and public knowledge, and long-sentence control, rhythm and wordplay may be only partly visible to me. The late very long novels may be uneven, and I cannot verify that. The inward, encyclopedic and often disturbing character of the project raises the open question of how the will's reference to an idealistic tendency applies. I do not treat that as settled in either direction. If the committee found, from Romanian-reading assessments, that the later volumes mainly repeat the early architecture, my case would weaken substantially. Yan Lianke would then be my first comparison, on narrative form and sustained imaginative force across decades. Carson would follow, on formal invention. Neither is a verified alternative, because for Yan Lianke I judge the Chinese register only through uneven translations, and for Carson I am unsure how far quality is spread across many volumes.

responses.point: Olsson keeps Carson as his first alternative and asks whether her hybridity is a core achievement or a series of brilliant experiments. He also says the will's idealistic tendency is a matter of interpretation that he does not treat as settled either way. He ranks Yan Lianke fifth because quality seems uneven across his titles.
responses.response: I share his refusal to settle the idealistic-tendency question by assertion, and I would add that it should be applied by one shared reading to every candidate, not only to the formally radical or ironic ones. On Carson I remain where I was. The question about the core oeuvre is the right one, and I would take original verse, verse narrative and essay as the core and the classical translations as context. Even then I cannot show sustained quality across many volumes, so she stays an alternative and not my choice. On Yan Lianke, his point about unevenness is fair. I would answer that a large body with uneven titles is not a flaw in itself if the best books carry a recognisable formal invention. The difficulty is that I cannot separate the strong books from the rest through translation, and I accept that this limits how far I can press the case.

responses.point: Mattson says that the late long novels may be uneven or excessive and that maximalist scale may limit breadth of significance. She keeps Murnane as her main alternative, citing restraint and rigorous form, and would turn to Murnane or Yan Lianke if the Cărtărescu case failed.
responses.response: I accept her length and unevenness concern as the fair test of my own case, and I cannot dismiss it. My reply is only that scale here is a structural choice and not padding. I cannot prove that from reception, and I do not claim to. On Murnane I agree that restraint is a real literary quality, and I did not rank him sixth for narrowness alone. Intensity is a legitimate virtue. My concern is the criterion of significance across a body of work, where a deliberately narrow project makes a smaller claim than one that joins the intimate to the encyclopedic. I would not dismiss her case, and I would hear it further if the committee finds Cărtărescu's late work repetitive. I agree with her that Yan Lianke has to be argued from narrative form, not from the circumstances of publication.

responses.point: Carlberg states that her central claim, linguistic distinctiveness, is the one she can least verify. She says a case resting on a few peaks rather than a spread of sustained quality would weaken. She ranks Yan Lianke third on narrative form but will not move him above Carson without a clearer account of consistency across his titles.
responses.response: Her honesty about the one claim she cannot verify applies to me as well, and I should state it plainly: the Romanian sentence is the thing I cannot test. Her peaks-versus-spread test is the right one, and the only evidence I can offer is that the public record shows several large works and a poetry and shorter-prose strand, not one book. That is reception evidence and not proof. On Yan Lianke I take her request seriously, and I would not claim more than I can show. A clearer account would separate the books that carry the mythorealist form (The Four Books, The Explosion Chronicles) from the weaker ones, and I cannot yet do that from public knowledge. That is why he is my first alternative and not above Cărtărescu.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg frames the Cărtărescu citation within the European tradition of inward and fantastic narrative. He asks whether the committee has Arabic-reading assessors who could settle what translation hides for Adonis. He also says the strong Yan Lianke books should be separated from the rest.
responses.response: I proposed that framing in round 1, and I now think it should be used cautiously. It places him in a tradition without making a regional claim, but it risks suggesting a European tie as a ground of merit. I have therefore softened the citation to describe the kind of imagination and not the tradition. His call for language-specific assessment is one I support for every case that depends on language texture, which includes Romanian as well as Arabic and Chinese. On Adonis my position is as in round 1: I ranked him seventh because his main formal influence seems to me to belong to earlier decades inside Arabic poetry, and I cannot judge recent sustained work. I would reconsider if assessments by readers of the Arabic showed that his later poems keep that level. His age is not a literary criterion.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's density, rhythm and long-sentence control survives translation. My view rests on public knowledge and reception, not on independent reading of the Romanian.
Whether the later very long novels, including Solenoid, deepen the early project or only extend it. I read the public record as showing development but cannot verify it.
Coverage of his poetry, early work and essays in translation is thinner than for the major novels, so the whole-oeuvre judgment leans on the novels.
How the will's reference to an idealistic tendency should be read for an inward, encyclopedic and often disturbing project, and whether one reading can be applied equally to every candidate.
For Yan Lianke, Carson and Adonis, sustained quality across many titles or decades cannot be established from translation, so my alternatives are not verified comparisons.
No independent verification of any source or corpus has been carried out.
statement.conflict_note: No change since round 1. The supplied profile records no personal or institutional connection to any shortlisted writer. I sit on the committee with the other five listed members, which is a disclosed institutional fact and not a connection to a candidate. My own practice as a novelist is context and not a ground for favouring any candidate. Carlberg's actual voting status is undocumented, and her simulated vote is a modeling assumption.
